papers.title: Visual Plant Imagery and Property Valuation: A Descriptive Analysis
papers.authors: Yuqian Chang, Nathan Fong, Ning Ye, Maureen (Mimi) Morrin
papers.abstract: Online home profiles with more plant imagery are associated with higher property valuations, even after accounting for extensive property, neighborhood, listing, and market factors.

papers.title: From Live to Recording: Consumer Demand and Response to Price Across the Livestreaming Lifecycle
papers.authors: Ziwei Cong, Jia Liu, Puneet Manchanda
papers.abstract: Using data from a knowledge-sharing platform that sells recorded versions of paid livestreams, this paper finds that demand is surprisingly more price sensitive before the event than after, which is explained partly by consumer self-selection and the lower quality uncertainty once the livestream ends.

papers.title: The Identification of the Dynamic Discrete-Choice Model with Stockpiling
papers.authors: Xinyao Kong, Jean-Pierre Dubé, Vaness Alwan
papers.abstract: We study the identification of the discount factor for dynamic discrete-choice (DDC) models of demand with stockpiling of a storable good. We show that the DDC has built-in exclusion restrictions that set-identify the discount factor without requiring any auxiliary assumptions. We compare this approach to previous work that assumes auxiliary structure on the storage cost function, clarifying how such structure generates exclusion restrictions and the corresponding data moments used for identification. Our key results show that these auxiliary restrictions are not necessary for identification; but that they are testable and can be included to achieve point identification and improve statistical efficiency. Using a case study of laundry detergent from earlier published work, we find a mean discount factor estimate of $0.957$, rejecting myopic models of choice in favor of the dynamic model. In counterfactual simulations, we show that some of the promotional lift during a discount period is indeed due to forward-buying. However, we predict considerably higher incremental sales compared to a standard discrete-choice model, which predicts that promotional discounts mainly cause substitution between brands. These results contribute to the long-standing discussion about the effectiveness of price promotions.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Lifestage Bias: How the Visual Representation of Product Lifespan Shapes Replacement Timing
papers.authors: Poornima Vinoo, Grant E. Donnelly, Mathew S. Isaac, Aaron R. Brough
papers.abstract:
To guide consumers’ decisions regarding when to replace products such as water filters, printer ink cartridges, and engine oil, companies often provide visualizations of the product’s lifespan. We document a
                    lifestage bias
                    in which representing a product’s lifespan with more (vs. fewer) visually distinct stages increases replacement intentions even when the product’s actual usage is the same. The effect emerges because a greater number of visually distinct stages leads consumers to mentally simulate previous use, thus enhancing the perception that a product has progressed through its lifespan and encouraging product replacement. Ten studies document lifestage bias and provide support (via mediation and moderation) for the underlying
                    usage simulation
                    mechanism. Notably, lifestage bias is eliminated when stages are represented non-visually or when stages are not visually distinct. Furthermore, lifestage bias is attenuated when product deterioration can be observed directly. These findings provide important insights into how consumers make product replacement timing decisions. Adjusting the number of distinct stages in product replacement guides offers firms and policymakers a practical tool to influence replacement timing—accelerating it when timely replacement is necessary for health, safety, or regulatory reasons (thus improving consumer welfare), or delaying it when items can be safely used for longer (thus reducing waste).

papers.title: EXPRESS: The Collecting Mindset: Viewing Purchasing as Collecting Enhances Acquisition Experience and Product Desirability
papers.authors: Elena Bocchi, Adam Eric Greenberg, Zachary Estes
papers.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Managers often struggle to make acquisition processes engaging. While the dominant approach to reducing search costs has been to streamline the acquisition process, seven preregistered studies plus one supplemental study (N = 3,306) reveal an alternative pathway: Prompting consumers to view purchasing as “collecting” by positioning products as additions to their own collections, rather than as ad hoc purchases, improves consumers’ acquisition experience and increases product desirability. The authors demonstrate that activating such a
                    collecting mindset
                    shifts consumers’ psychological focus of the shopping process from securing a standalone product to instead investing in advancing their collection, thereby making them derive positive experience utility from the process, and in turn, elevating the desirability of the sought products. This research also offers practical guidance on how marketers can maximize the effectiveness of activating a collecting mindset: (i) encouraging active engagement in search, (ii) ensuring that search yields products that meaningfully advance the collection, and (iii) aligning the collection with an identity consumers value, as the effect may otherwise attenuate or reverse. These findings advance theory on everyday collecting and consumer search, and show how retailers and brands can strategically turn purchasing into a more positive acquisition experience that enhances product desirability.
